I've been thinking on the issue of modding subverses/subreddits for a little while and I wanted to share my thoughts. There are a few relevant problems that we need to manage if we're going to reach a set of guidelines that we're all satisfied with.

----------------

1). Voat is built on the principle of free expression.

We, as a community, are committed to allowing the expression of all points of view. Voat's motto is "have your say", and many of us came here because we're concerned about censorship of free expression on Reddit. However, the fact is that in this era there are some individuals who's point of view is that free expression is undesirable.

This leaves us with an apparent paradox. Those who do not believe in free expression do not share the values of our community, and so it follows they should be expelled from the community. However, expelling those who do not share our perspective runs contrary to the stated commitment to freedom of expression. As a community, we must answer the following question: "are we willing to tolerate the presence of those who want to undermine our community?"

2). Identifying people's intent on the internet is hard.

Is @she a person who would undermine the principles of Voat? Honestly I don't know. How would we know? In reference to the first problem, how would the community go about identifying any user who would want to undermine our principles? The drama surrounding @she is only an example, we need to seek a solution to the more general problem.

Let's be reasonable, it's impractical and inappropriate to scrutinize people's comment histories for "evidence" that they think a certain way. And even if we could and did, who would be in a position to determine if any given user actually adheres to the "principles of the community"? Who among us has the authority to judge "our principles" and apply them to others? I certainly don't, and frankly even @atko doesn't have the right to do so.

Do we hold votes? A monthly vote of confidence in the mods? Because all internet polls are infallible, right? We all know that the vote proclaiming moot was the most influential person in the world in 2009 was totally legit, right? If an organized cabal even exists on Voat, we can only assume that votes of this kind would invariably be compromised. Not only that, but it turns us into a mob who goes on regular witch-hunts.

So if nobody is in a position to make individual assessments, and group assessments are unreasonable, what are we left with?

3) Communities need both rules and leaders/mods to enforce them.

I've been in charge of an online community. I've written extremely harsh rules and enforced them with absolutely no flexibility, and I have no problem saying so. Groups have rules because without those rules the group cannot achieve it's goals. Sometimes you need harsh rules to meet your goals, other times you don't. A good leader knows what rules need to be enforced strictly and which ones do not, and different communities on Voat will require different rules with different degrees of strictness to reach their particular goals. The Voat community as a whole cannot get in an uproar every time a harsh rule is enforced.

That said, all rules need justification. And harsh rules need excellent justification. When a harsh rule exists with poor justification, you get the drama we've seen in /v/AskVoat. The mark of a good leader or mod is that they can provide the necessary justification for harsh rules when required, and that they amend harsh rules when those rules lack justification. The community needs a recourse when mods do not do this.

----------------

These are my observations. I do not have suggestions to resolve them all.

I do have one suggestion that may help: Create a new tool focused on addressing grievances between mods and their communities.

I propose a button on each subverse page accessible only to subscribed non-moderators for that sub. To press the button, the account must be subscribed to that sub for at least a month, and each account is limited to pressing the button once per month. The button opens a page where the user can submit something like mod mail where they can address their concern either to a particular mod or to all the mods for that sub. There, they can ask questions about rules or the application of rules and get a response from a mod. This function would be anonymous from the mod's perspective, they would be unable to see which account asked the question. After receiving their answer, the user would rate their satisfaction with the mod response.

This tool would help mods keep tabs on the needs and concerns of their community without having hordes of off-topic posts and drama all over the subverse. Modmail would still be used for general communication with the mods about reporting issues, suggestions, or general concerns. And users will have their use of the grievance feature tracked and "excessive complainers" may be banned from using the site-wide function.

The logs of these grievances would naturally be accessible to the admins of Voat. When a particular subverse gets a "large number" of complaints, and when the responses to those complaints are received with low satisfaction, then a message is automatically sent to the admins for personal evaluation. They can look through the questions asked, the answers provided, and the ratings given. I do trust @atko to reasonably identify when a large number of bogus complaints are filed and when they are given inappropriately low satisfaction ratings. If it appears that organized brigading has occurred, then the admins can ignore it.

If it seems there are a large number of legitimate concerns that have not received appropriate responses, then the admins can communicate with the existing mods of the subverse to help remedy the situation.

----------------

I'd love to hear your thoughts both on the three major problems I've identified, and on my proposed solution.
Subverse Grievance Button: A proposed solution to the recent moderation problems. [Plus a few discussion points]
